Let’s step into Chapter 1: Childhood in a City of Shadows and Light.
Have you ever noticed how a city can almost feel alive—like it’s holding onto its own memories? For a child growing up in Istanbul, that feeling is everywhere. It’s as much a part of daily life as the call to prayer rolling through the streets, echoing off those domes and minarets on the skyline. These shapes, so grand and ancient to visitors, are just the scenery of everyday life to a young mind. But the city’s beauty is tangled up with a sense of loss—woven together in a way that shapes every memory and every way of seeing the world.
Inside a small family apartment, there’s a quiet tension. It hangs in the air, thick with unspoken worries. Here, a boy learns to read the moods of adults just as closely as he watches the changing weather outside the window. The rooms are lined with old photographs, wallpaper faded by time, and every object seems to carry a story—one that’s never really been told. And outside? The city feels both inviting and mysterious, promising adventure around every corner, but also carrying a sadness that’s hard to put into words.
Most mornings start with the simple rituals of family life: the clatter of breakfast dishes, parents bickering softly, a distant radio bringing news that seems stuck on repeat. The boy’s father is present, but in a way, he’s not really there—his thoughts always somewhere else. Sometimes he vanishes for days, leaving an uncertainty that settles over the home like a layer of dust. The mother, practical and quietly strong, holds everything together. Her patience is tested daily—by the city’s unpredictability, and by the family’s own struggles.
Step outside, and Istanbul bursts into life with all its contradictions. The Bosphorus sparkles in the morning sun, ferries glide across the water, and seagulls swoop overhead. But just a few streets away, you’ll find crumbling mansions and overgrown gardens, silent reminders of a time when this city was the center of an empire. Now, it sits somewhere between remembering its glorious past and coming to terms with a faded present. Children laugh and play in alleys lined with broken stones, their voices bouncing off walls that have seen far better days.
For a child, these contrasts are both confusing and completely fascinating. It always feels like Istanbul is about to reveal a secret—if you just know where to look. Wandering through old neighborhoods, the boy is drawn to ruins and empty lots, places where history feels close enough to reach out and touch. He imagines the lives of those who once lived in the grand houses—people whose fortunes were lost to time and circumstance.
Family gatherings at home are filled with stories about the past. Uncles and aunts remember when Istanbul was a city of promise, their voices colored with both pride and regret. The boy listens, trying to piece together a history that feels at once deeply personal and impossibly far away. And he begins to realize—this sadness he senses in the city isn’t just his. It’s something everyone in Istanbul seems to carry.
As the seasons shift, so does the city. Winters bring a damp chill that settles in your bones, and in summer, the air is thick with the scent of jasmine and the calls of street vendors drifting through the windows. Through it all, the boy learns to see Istanbul not just as a place, but almost as a living memory—a city built on loss, resilience, and the quiet hope that even amid ruins, something beautiful might still be found.
In these early years, the city’s melancholy becomes his companion. It’s there in the hush after an argument, in the empty rooms of once-grand homes, and in the golden light that stretches across the Bosphorus at dusk. This feeling—so tough to name—starts to shape how he sees himself, and his place in the world. And slowly, he understands: to truly love Istanbul, you have to accept its sadness too. You find meaning in the shadows, just as much as the light.
